query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: If FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy feedstock (15–45 μm) is sprayed using the HVAF-i7 torch with a nozzle-to-substrate distance optimized to 300–350 mm, then the increased particle velocity will lead to enhanced deposition efficiency and a significantly thicker, adherent bond coat with minimal as-sprayed oxidation, even when coating internal diameters as small as 120 mm.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a feedstock size distribution of 15–45 μm, previously shown to yield high-quality coatings using HVAF-M3.
generation.intervention: Adjust the nozzle-to-substrate distance on the HVAF-i7 system to 300–350 mm while keeping all other deposition parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Deposition conducted under standard HVAF-i7 operating conditions onto substrates (including those with internal diameters as small as 120 mm) that have been properly prepared (e.g., cleaned, roughened) to promote adhesion.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced kinetic energy of the particles at impact, which improves splat flattening, intersplat bonding, and overall deposition efficiency.
generation.mechanism: At a nozzle-to-substrate distance of 300–350 mm, particles have a reduced dwell time in the heated gas stream yet maintain sufficient velocity to impact the substrate forcefully. This higher kinetic energy promotes better deformation and bonding of the splats, resulting in a denser, thicker coating while avoiding excessive in-flight oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline HVAF-i7 coatings produced at non-optimized distances, the coating thickness will significantly increase (targeting a level comparable to or exceeding that produced by the HVAF-M3 torch) while maintaining high adhesion and minimal as-sprayed oxidation, ensuring durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service.
generation.baseline: HVAF-i7 sprayed coatings using 15–45 μm feedstock at standard (non-optimized) nozzle-to-substrate distances, which yield acceptable quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: The optimized spray distance should remain effective for substrates with internal diameters down to 120 mm and under typical thermal barrier service conditions. Deviations significantly outside the 300–350 mm range may lead to increased in-flight oxidation (if too long) or insufficient melting/deposition (if too short).
generation.uncertainty: Potential variability may arise from modified plume dynamics in confined internal geometries and interactions with gas flow, which might necessitate fine-tuning of additional parameters (such as gas flow rate or torch power) to fully achieve the desired thickness.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of HVAF-i7 depositions using FeCoNiCrAl 15–45 μm feedstock at varying nozzle-to-substrate distances (e.g., 250 mm, 300 mm, 350 mm, and 400 mm) on standard substrates as well as on substrates with a 120 mm internal diameter. Assess the resulting coating thickness, as-sprayed oxidation level, and adhesion.
measurements: Coating thickness via cross-sectional microscopy (e.g., SEM)
Oxidation level via EDS/XRD analysis of the coating surface and cross-section
Adhesion strength via standardized pull-off tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if, after optimizing to a 300–350 mm nozzle-to-substrate distance, there is no statistically significant increase in coating thickness compared to the baseline, or if the as-sprayed oxidation and adhesion degrade beyond acceptable limits. In other words, if the optimized distance does not yield a thicker, durable coating with minimal oxidation, the hypothesis is not supported.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. Oxidation and Phase Transformations in the Powder during HVOF Spraying
cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Characterization of the Raw Material of Powder and Sprayed Coatings
cited_evidence.text: The surface and cross-section morphology of the sprayed HECs can be seen in Figure 2. Figure 2a,b show the surface topography, which had an overall uneven appearance typical of coatings subjected to plasma spraying. There were island-like and protruded tissues as well as smooth tissues on the surface. These island-like ones were formed by the semi-solid deposition of partially melted large-size and medium-size powder particles, while smooth ones were formed by completely melted liquid deposition. Figure 2c,d show the cross-section morphology of the coating. It can be seen that the coating had a thickness of about 250 μm and a typical layered structure. It looked even and compact, had a few pores and had experienced slight oxidation, but no cracks were observed. Some undulations could be seen on the surface. The coating was well bonded with the substrate, showing mechanical bonding. The XRD pattern in Figure 3a shows that the phase composition of the coating after spraying was consistent with that of the powder, indicating that the spraying process had not changed the phase structure of the coating.

papers.title: In-situ CrFeCoNi medium entropy alloying coating via electrospark powder deposition.
papers.system: CrFeCoNi medium‐entropy alloy coatings on A516 steel by electrospark deposition
papers.approach: Using powder feedstock in an electrospark deposition process with controlled electrical parameters
papers.findings: At lower electrical settings, most powders fuse but some remain unmelted; process parameters (e.g., pulse energy, voltage) are critical to achieving good bonding and fusion.
papers.mechanism: High local temperatures generated by sparks melt and fuse the powder particles. Insufficient energy (voltage) leaves unmelted particles and gaps between splats.

papers.title: Effects of Nano-CeO2 on Microstructure and Properties of WC/FeCoNiCrMo0.2 Composite High Entropy Alloy Coatings by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: WC/FeCoNiCrMo0.2 composite HEA coatings deposited by laser cladding on stainless steel
papers.approach: Introducing nano-CeO2 into the feedstock and using coaxial powder feeding during laser cladding
papers.findings: Addition of 2% CeO2 resulted in coatings free of obvious bubbles and cracks, with improved bonding and lower dilution due to a more controlled molten pool.
papers.mechanism: The rare-earth element Ce preferentially combines with oxygen in the melt pool, reducing pore formation and stabilizing the molten pool, which aids in forming a denser coating.

papers.title: Initial Oxidation Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Coating Produced by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying in the Range of 650 °C to 1000 °C.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coatings prepared by atmospheric plasma spraying
papers.approach: Deposition via APS with analysis of surface and cross-sectional morphology after oxidation at various temperatures
papers.findings: Coatings achieved a thickness of about 250 μm with typical lamellar structure and slight oxidation; phase composition remained consistent with the starting powder.
papers.mechanism: Rapid plasma heating and subsequent quenching lead to a layered (splat) structure with minimal oxidation if conditions are carefully controlled.

papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder used for HVOF deposition
papers.approach: Spraying powder at various nozzle-to-substrate distances; examining the impact on porosity, oxide content, and phase transformation
papers.findings: Longer spraying distances decrease kinetic energy, leading to increased porosity and oxidation. There is a trade‐off between particle dwell time (and thus oxidation) and impact energy needed for dense deposition.
papers.mechanism: Shorter spray distances maintain higher particle velocity and reduce in-flight oxidation, while longer distances allow more oxygen exposure and reduced particle momentum.

established: Optimal feedstock size (15–45 μm) with the HVAF-M3 torch can produce high-quality, dense coatings.
Elevated particle velocity (achieved at specific spray distances, e.g., 300–350 mm) improves deposition efficiency for conventional MCrAlY bond coats.

approaches_tried.approach: Using a 15–45 μm feedstock with the HVAF-M3 system
approaches_tried.outcome: Produced high-quality coatings with good integrity and minimal oxidation under optimized conditions.

approaches_tried.approach: Applying the same feedstock and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch
approaches_tried.outcome: Yielded acceptable coating quality but resulted in inadequate thickness, likely due to differences in particle velocity or spray dynamics.

approaches_tried.approach: Optimizing spray distance for conventional MCrAlY bond coats (best at 300–350 mm)
approaches_tried.outcome: A slight gain in deposition efficiency was observed, suggesting that particle velocity is critical in achieving thicker coatings.

mechanisms: Higher particle velocity increases the kinetic energy of individual feedstock particles, resulting in better splat flattening and adhesion, which in turn enhances deposition efficiency and coating thickness.
Spray distance directly affects particle dwell time in the hot gas stream; an optimal distance maintains high enough velocity while limiting in-flight oxidation.
disagreements: Some studies indicate that increasing spray distance could lead to higher oxidation due to longer oxygen exposure, while others emphasize that a carefully optimized distance improves deposition efficiency by providing higher particle momentum.
open_questions: Can increasing particle velocity by optimizing the spray distance (e.g., to 300–350 mm) in the HVAF-i7 system overcome the thickness limitation without incurring detrimental oxidation effects?
How will the optimized deposition parameters scale for coatings applied inside small internal diameters (down to 120 mm) where geometric constraints might affect the spray dynamics?
opportunities: Testing the single intervention of increasing particle velocity via an optimized nozzle-to-substrate distance (300–350 mm) in the HVAF-i7 system to achieve thicker bond coats.
Evaluating the as-sprayed oxidation levels and mechanical adhesion under high-temperature thermal-barrier service conditions in confined (120 mm internal diameter) geometries.
Combining a higher particle velocity intervention with other process controls (e.g., gas atmospheres or secondary energy input) to further limit oxidation while enhancing deposition thickness.

directions.direction: Optimize the nozzle-to-substrate distance on the HVAF-i7 torch to increase particle velocity.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the thickness limitation by raising particle kinetic energy at impact, which improves splat flattening and deposition efficiency. This intervention is supported by conventional MCrAlY work that showed best spray distances of 300–350 mm, and it respects the use of the established 15–45 μm feedstock. It is both feasible and informative.

directions.direction: Increase torch power or energy input on the HVAF-i7 system.
directions.assessment: While raising the power may improve particle momentum and melting, it risks excessive in-flight oxidation and may require significant equipment changes. It is less directly aligned with the observed success from optimized spray distance in conventional systems.

directions.direction: Modify the feedstock morphology (e.g., using a narrower size distribution or spherodized particles) to enhance deposition mass per particle.
directions.assessment: Although a modified particle shape might improve deposition efficiency, the current feedstock (15–45 μm) is already optimal for quality. Changing the morphology could compromise coating integrity or oxidation resistance, and would not be as direct an intervention to solve the thickness issue observed with the HVAF-i7 torch.

directions.direction: Introduce an inert gas shroud or adjust gas composition to reduce in-flight oxidation while allowing thicker deposits.
directions.assessment: Improving the gas atmosphere may help reduce oxidation, but it does not directly address the inability to build enough thickness. This adds process complexity and may interfere with the current good quality of the as-sprayed coating.

directions.direction: Preheat the substrate to promote better splat substrate bonding and enable thicker builds.
directions.assessment: Substrate preheating could improve adhesion, yet it does not inherently increase the kinetic energy of the particles arriving from the HVAF-i7 torch. As such, it is less directly targeted at overcoming the specific thickness limitation.

choice.direction: Optimize the nozzle-to-substrate distance on the HVAF-i7 torch (targeting 300–350 mm) to increase particle velocity.
choice.why: This intervention builds directly on the evidence that higher particle velocity, achieved by adjusting the spray distance in conventional MCrAlY coatings, improves deposition efficiency. Since the HVAF-i7 application with the standard 15–45 μm feedstock suffers from inadequate thickness, this single change is expected to boost the kinetic energy of the particles, thereby increasing coating build-up without sacrificing coating integrity or oxidation resistance.
